---
title: "NIH data management and sharing"
order: 157
---

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The short version
- **Finish line:** you can explain NIH's Data Management and Sharing (DMS) policy, why it reaches REDS
  through contracts, where shared data ends up, and what Lakeshore's IT has to support: a transfer
  ledger, provenance, retention terms and a correction path.
- **Punchline:** the hub's draft data agreement lets the program share data "in NIH-designated
  repositories." The Director's decision: Lakeshore accepts repository sharing only of data the
  program has **further de-identified under its own process**, never Lakeshore's coded key or crosswalk.
  The DUA (data use agreement) names retention and destruction terms, and IT builds the ledger and
  provenance record as part of EXT-21.
- **The rule in one line:** the DMS policy binds NIH-funded researchers and institutions, here the
  hubs, DCC and CTLS under their contracts. It does not bind Lakeshore directly. Lakeshore feels it
  through what its agreement passes down, so read the agreement as the real rule.
- **Monday question:** "For the last file EXT-21 sent: which spec version, which mapping version,
  what checksum, and where is the receipt?"
- **The trap:** assuming "NIH sharing" means Lakeshore's limited data set goes public. It doesn't,
  unless the DUA lets it, and Lakeshore decides that in the DUA.
:::

## The clause

The hub's draft data agreement arrives for RSH-0107. Regulatory affairs flags a single sentence on
page six. Among the permitted uses of the data, the agreement allows "sharing in NIH-designated
repositories consistent with the NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy."

The privacy officer is first at your desk, printout in hand. "I signed off on a limited data set
going to the hub for the program's research. I did not sign off on it going into a public
repository. Does this clause let it?"

The medical director, who has just read the clause: "That's NIH's policy. Everyone sharing data
under NIH money has to do it. It would be strange for us to object."

The systems administrator: "If the data's going to a repository anyway, why are we fussing over
retention? They keep it."

Your Quality Analyst asks the quiet question: "When the hub asks us, two years from now, which
version of the mapping produced a file, can we answer?"

Four people, four assumptions: that the policy binds Lakeshore, that sharing means public, that
someone else's retention is enough, and that provenance is the program's problem. This lesson pulls
them apart, using the policy's own text, and ends with the decision you record in RSH-0107.

## What the policy is, and who it binds

NIH's Policy for Data Management and Sharing (NOT-OD-21-013, here "the DMS policy") is a **funding
policy**. It is not a regulation in the Code of Federal Regulations. It becomes binding the way
funding conditions do: through the award. Our local copy is in
`sources/nih/dms-policy-not-od-21-013.md`, and the copy's own header says it binds funded
researchers and institutions, and is not binding on a blood center that isn't an NIH awardee or
performing under one.

Its idea is simple. Before researchers generate data, they write a **plan** for how they will manage
it and share it. NIH approves the plan. Then they follow it. The policy does not say "share
everything." In its discussion section NIH says the final policy "does not create a uniform
requirement to share all scientific data," and expects researchers to "maximize appropriate data
sharing" while accounting for legal, ethical or technical limits.

The ITSM bridge is a **service level agreement written before the service starts**. The researcher
commits in advance to what will be preserved, where, and under what limits. The funder holds them to
it. Lakeshore's equivalent is a service contract you didn't write but will be measured against.

## How it reaches REDS, and where Lakeshore sits

Module 1 laid out the contract chain: NIH contracts to hubs, a DCC (Data Coordinating Center) and a
CTLS (Center for Transfusion Laboratory Studies), and the hubs invite blood centers to contribute.
The DMS policy's scope section says it applies to research funded by "extramural grants, contracts,
Intramural Research Projects, or other funding agreements." The REDS records are **contracts**, so
the policy's contract language is the relevant text: the plan "will become a Term and Condition of
the Award, and compliance with and enforcement of the Plan will be consistent with the award and the
Federal Acquisition Regulations, as applicable."

Three honest points about where that leaves Lakeshore:

1. **The obligated parties are the funded ones.** The hubs, DCC and CTLS submit and follow plans.
   Lakeshore, as a contributing blood center, is not the awardee of the REDS contracts.
2. **Whether the policy covers the current round isn't something our sources prove.** The policy's
   effective date covers "proposals for contracts that are submitted to NIH on or after January 25,
   2023." The contract records we hold are the 2026 RePORTER entries from module 1; they say nothing
   about when proposals were submitted or what plans were approved. It would be reasonable to expect
   the hubs operate under a plan. The Director's move is to **ask**, not assume: "Is there an
   NIH-approved Data Management and Sharing Plan for this program phase, and which parts of it
   touch data we contribute?"
3. **Lakeshore's exposure is whatever the agreement passes down.** The policy itself says nothing
   about subawardees' or contributors' duties. If the hub's agreement says "Lakeshore will comply
   with the program's data management and sharing plan," then Lakeshore has accepted it
   contractually. That is a contract obligation, not an NIH one, and you read it as one.

## How a contributing blood center feels it anyway

A researcher who must produce a plan and keep to it will ask contributors for what the plan needs.
Expect four kinds of request, and notice that every one lands on IT:

- **Agreement terms** that permit sharing, name repositories or set retention (the clause on page six).
- **Provenance and documentation requests.** The policy's own definition of metadata includes "data
  provenance" and "data transformations." The program needs to be able to say where a value came
  from and what was done to it.
- **Retention of what you sent.** If a study is later re-analyzed or a repository question comes up,
  someone asks what exactly Lakeshore contributed.
- **Correction handling.** Data that will be shared should be right. Errors found downstream come
  back to the source.

There is also the program's own statement of how it treats data. The 2022 design paper says "The
source data are retained allowing for potential new analyses or investigations without the need for
additional data extractions." Read that as the program's design, not a Lakeshore obligation. But it
tells you what you send will outlive the study that asked for it.

## Where shared data ends up

The sources are thin here, and the lesson says so rather than guessing. What we have:

- **The paper says** investigators have explored "the public-use version of the REDS-III V2V
  database (accessed through BioLINCC)." BioLINCC is the NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood
  Institute) repository for study data and specimens. So for the earlier program round, the paper
  documents a path from the V2V database to a public-use version in an NHLBI repository.
- **The DMS policy** says it "strongly encourages the use of established repositories" and points
  researchers to NIH's repository-selection guidance. It names no REDS repository.
- **What we don't have:** a REDS-IV-P or current-round plan, or any statement of what will be
  shared, in what form, or when. This lesson invents none. The Director asks the hub for it.

Notice the shape, though. "Public-use" implies a **version prepared for sharing**, not the raw
contributions. Data moves from contributed records, to the program's database, to a prepared
version, to a repository. Each hop is a decision, and the decision belongs to the program, within
the limits the agreements set. Lakeshore's decision is what its DUA allows at the first hop and
beyond.

## Why this matters, and the plain-English rule

The failure to prevent is **loss of control over a donor-derived dataset**. A limited data set still
contains dates and sometimes geography, and a coded key plus a crosswalk can re-link a code to a
person. If an agreement lets data flow onward with only "consistent with NIH policy" as the limit,
Lakeshore has handed its privacy decision to a policy that, by its own words, doesn't add privacy
protections.

In plain English:

1. **The DMS policy obligates the funded researchers and institutions.** It requires a plan and
   compliance with the approved plan.
2. **It doesn't change the human-subjects or privacy rules.** NIH says in its discussion that the
   policy "does not introduce new requirements for protections for research with human
   participants," and that existing laws, regulations and policies "continue to apply." Lakeshore's
   HIPAA basis is still its own limited data set and DUA, from
   [module 3](../human-subjects-hipaa-and-certificates-of-confidentiality/index.qmd).
3. **"Sharing" is a spectrum.** A limited data set shared under a DUA is not a public file.
   Public sharing would require the program to de-identify further, and that is not Lakeshore's call
   to make, but Lakeshore's DUA must say so.
4. **Lakeshore's IT supports what the agreement and plan need**: a transfer ledger, provenance,
   retention of what was sent and of the crosswalk per the DUA, and a way to handle corrections.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIH, NOT-OD-21-013, Section II | "the DMS policy, section two, definitions" | Funding policy: defines scientific data, data management, data sharing, metadata, plan | What "sharing" and "provenance" mean in the program's own plan |
| NOT-OD-21-013, Section III | "section three, scope" | Funding policy: applies to research funded or conducted by NIH, including contracts | Why the hubs, DCC and CTLS are covered |
| NOT-OD-21-013, Section V | "section five, requirements" | Funding policy: submit a plan and comply with the approved plan | What the program owes NIH |
| NOT-OD-21-013, Section VI | "section six, plans" | Funding policy: plans are part of a contract's technical evaluation | How the plan enters the REDS contracts |
| NOT-OD-21-013, Section VII | "section seven" | Funding policy: expectations on human-participant data, repositories, timelines | The repository and "no later than publication" timing |
| NOT-OD-21-013, Section VIII | "section eight, compliance" | Funding policy: for contracts, the plan becomes a term and condition | How the plan binds the performers |
| 45 CFR 164.514(e)(4) | "one-sixty-four point five-fourteen, e, four" | HIPAA regulation: what a data use agreement must contain | What Lakeshore's DUA must say about onward disclosure |
| 45 CFR 164.514(e)(2) | "...e, two" | HIPAA regulation: the direct identifiers a limited data set excludes | Why EXT-21 output can contain dates but not names or addresses |
| 21 CFR 606.160(d) | "six-oh-six point one-sixty, d" | Regulation: retention of blood product records | The BECS records; not the extract file |
| Josephson et al., *Transfusion* 2022 | "the REDS-IV-P design paper" | Peer-reviewed program description | Source data retained; REDS-III public-use data through BioLINCC |

## The actual text

All quotes below are verbatim from `sources/nih/dms-policy-not-od-21-013.md` unless marked.

**Section II, the definitions that matter to IT:**

> Scientific Data: The recorded factual material commonly accepted in the scientific community as of
> sufficient quality to validate and replicate research findings, regardless of whether the data are
> used to support scholarly publications. Scientific data do not include laboratory notebooks,
> preliminary analyses, completed case report forms, drafts of scientific papers, plans for future
> research, peer reviews, communications with colleagues, or physical objects, such as laboratory
> specimens.

> Data Sharing: The act of making scientific data available for use by others (e.g., the larger
> research community, institutions, the broader public), for example, via an established repository.

> Metadata: Data that provide additional information intended to make scientific data interpretable
> and reusable (e.g., date, independent sample and variable construction and description,
> methodology, data provenance, data transformations, any intermediate or descriptive observational
> variables).

*What it means here.* "Of sufficient quality" is the quality hook: data that can't be trusted isn't
scientific data. The sharing definition spans "institutions" to "the broader public," which is why
"sharing" in the clause could mean very different things. And the metadata definition names
**provenance** and **transformations**, which are exactly what EXT-21's mapping document and ledger
record. Physical objects such as specimens are excluded, so the retained donation samples in
rapid-response studies are not "scientific data" under the definition, though data generated from
them would be.

**Section III, scope:**

> The DMS Policy applies to all research, funded or conducted in whole or in part by NIH, that
> results in the generation of scientific data. This includes research funded or conducted by
> extramural grants, contracts, Intramural Research Projects, or other funding agreements regardless
> of NIH funding level or funding mechanism. The DMS Policy does not apply to research and other
> activities that do not generate scientific data, including training, infrastructure development,
> and non-research activities.

*What it means here.* "Contracts" are named. REDS is a set of contracts, so the policy can reach it.
The exclusion of "infrastructure development" and "non-research activities" is why you ask the hub
which activities are under the plan. Phase 3 abstracts mention dissemination and database closure
(module 1), and you shouldn't guess how those map.

**Section IV, effective date (the part about contracts):**

> The effective date of the DMS Policy is January 25, 2023, including for: [...] Proposals for
> contracts that are submitted to NIH on or after January 25, 2023;

*What it means here.* The trigger for contracts is the **proposal date**, not the award date. The
RePORTER records don't give it. Ask.

**Section V, requirements:**

> The DMS Policy requires:
> Submission of a Data Management and Sharing Plan outlining how scientific data and any
> accompanying metadata will be managed and shared, taking into account any potential restrictions
> or limitations.
> Compliance with the awardee's plan as approved by the NIH ICO.

*What it means here.* Two duties, both on the awardee: submit a plan, follow it. "Any potential
restrictions or limitations" is where a contributor's DUA terms belong. A restriction nobody tells
the program about can't be in the plan.

**Section VI, plans for contracts, and Section VIII, enforcement:**

> Plans will be included as part of the technical evaluation performed by NIH staff.

> Contracts: The Plan will become a Term and Condition of the Award, and compliance with and
> enforcement of the Plan will be consistent with the award and the Federal Acquisition Regulations,
> as applicable.

*What it means here.* For a contract, the plan is part of what NIH evaluates and then a term of the
award. That is why the hub may need things from Lakeshore: its own contract compliance depends on it.

**Section VII, human-participant data, limits and timing:**

> Any potential limitations on subsequent data use should be communicated to individuals or entities
> (e.g., data repository managers) that will preserve and share the scientific data.

> Applicable federal, Tribal, state, and local laws, regulations, statutes, guidance, and
> institutional policies govern research involving human participants and the sharing and use of
> scientific data derived from human participants. [...] Researchers proposing to generate scientific
> data derived from human participants should outline in their Plans how privacy, rights, and
> confidentiality of human research participants will be protected (i.e., through de-identification,
> Certificates of Confidentiality, and other protective measures).

> Shared scientific data should be made accessible as soon as possible, and no later than the time of
> an associated publication, or the end of performance period, whichever comes first.

*What it means here.* First: limitations travel with the data. If Lakeshore's DUA limits onward use,
the program should pass that to any repository. Second: de-identification and Certificates of
Confidentiality are named as the protective measures. Third: the **timeline** is a clock the program
runs. "Whichever comes first" means sharing can be due before the final paper. The wording is
"should," and it is about when shared data becomes accessible, not about how long Lakeshore keeps its
own copy. The policy separately encourages researchers to consider "data repository policies, award
record retention requirements, journal policies" as guidance for the minimum availability period.

**The policy's statement on human-participant protections.** This one is in NIH's discussion of
public comments, the preamble to the policy, not in the numbered policy sections:

> As with the Draft Policy, the final DMS Policy does not introduce new requirements for protections
> for research with human participants. Existing laws (e.g., Certificates of Confidentiality),
> regulations (e.g., the Common Rule), and policies (e.g., the NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy)
> continue to apply.

*What it means here.* The policy doesn't create privacy protection, and it doesn't waive any. Your privacy
analysis from module 3 stands.

**45 CFR 164.514(e)(4), what a data use agreement must say** (from
`sources/cfr/45-164-research-provisions-excerpt.md`):

> (A) Establish the permitted uses and disclosures of such information by the limited data set
> recipient, consistent with paragraph (e)(3) of this section. The data use agreement may not
> authorize the limited data set recipient to use or further disclose the information in a manner
> that would violate the requirements of this subpart, if done by the covered entity;
>
> (B) Establish who is permitted to use or receive the limited data set; and
>
> (C) Provide that the limited data set recipient will:
> (*1*) Not use or further disclose the information other than as permitted by the data use agreement
> or as otherwise required by law;
> (*2*) Use appropriate safeguards [...]
> (*3*) Report to the covered entity any use or disclosure of the information not provided for by its
> data use agreement of which it becomes aware;
> (*4*) Ensure that any agents to whom it provides the limited data set agree to the same
> restrictions and conditions [...]; and
> (*5*) Not identify the information or contact the individuals.

*What it means here.* This is the clause-by-clause test for the page-six sentence. "Consistent with
the NIH policy" doesn't "establish who is permitted to use or receive" the data. A repository's open
users aren't named in the DUA. (B) wants named recipients. (C)(1) says no further disclosure beyond
the agreement. (C)(4) pushes the same restrictions to agents. Subparagraph (e)(4)(iii) adds that a
covered entity that knew of a pattern of material breach by the recipient must take reasonable
steps to cure it, and if that fails, stop disclosing and report to the Secretary. So Lakeshore has
a continuing duty to the DUA, not just a signature.

**Not quoted, and why.** HIPAA's de-identification standard is at 45 CFR 164.514(a) and (b). Our
local privacy excerpt lists it as "not saved," so the lesson doesn't quote it. It is the right place
for the privacy officer to ground the word "de-identified" if the program proposes to share publicly.
Whether the program's own process meets that standard is the program's determination, and Lakeshore
should ask what process it follows.

## What "sharing" means for a limited data set

Put the decoder on one page:

| If the data is... | Who may have it | Who decides |
|---|---|---|
| EXT-21 output, a limited data set | The recipients the DUA names, for the purposes it names | Lakeshore, in the DUA |
| The same data, onward to the DCC, CTLS or other hubs | Only if the DUA names them or allows agents with the same restrictions | Lakeshore, in the DUA |
| A version the program has **further de-identified** under its own process | A repository's users, under that repository's terms | The program, with the DUA saying Lakeshore accepts this only for data de-identified this way |
| Lakeshore's coded key or crosswalk | Nobody outside Lakeshore | Lakeshore, always |
| Anything else "NIH-designated repository" language might sweep in | Nobody, until the DUA says so | Lakeshore, in the DUA |

The privacy officer's point is the third row. Public sharing would require the program to de-identify
further, and it is the program's call whether and how. But Lakeshore's DUA must say that without
further de-identification the data doesn't go to a repository. Silence is how a clause like page six
becomes permission.

The Certificates of Confidentiality decision from module 3 matters here. Lakeshore treats EXT-21
output and the crosswalk as covered information: no disclosure outside the research purpose, legal
requests to counsel, copies tracked, protection treated as indefinite. "Copies tracked" is the
sentence IT must turn into a ledger. "Indefinite" is why destruction terms in a DUA don't end the
protection.

## What Lakeshore's IT must support

None of the following is required by the DMS policy, which names no duty for a contributor. These
are the capabilities that the DUA, the privacy decisions and honest provenance need. Treat them as
Lakeshore's own design decisions, flagged as such.

### 1. The transfer ledger

One row per file sent. Fields:

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| Run ID and date/time of release | Ties to the signed QC checklist and reconciliation report (module 2) |
| File name and size | Identifies the artifact |
| **Spec version** | Which approved data specification defined the contents |
| **Mapping version** | Which field-mapping document produced the columns |
| Row counts per table | Compare to the reconciliation report |
| **Checksum** (and the algorithm) | Proves the file received is the file released |
| Recipient and transfer method | Matches the DUA's named recipients |
| Receipt reference | The hub's acknowledgment, per module 2's transfer step |
| Superseded-by / supersedes | Links a corrected file to the one it replaces |

The ITSM bridge is **configuration management applied to a data release**: every released file is a
release record you can reproduce or explain. The ledger is also how Lakeshore tracks "copies" for the
Certificates of Confidentiality decision.

### 2. Provenance

Provenance answers: **which BECS fields, through which mapping version, in which run**. Module 2 made
the mapping document and the CMDB relationships between EXT-21 and its source fields. This lesson adds
the join: each ledger row points to the mapping version in force, and each mapping version to the
source fields and the BECS release at the time. When BECS changes (module 6), the join tells you
which past files were produced under the old mapping. Provenance is not a promise about the BECS
records themselves. Those remain under their own controls and the ALCOA principles in
[ALCOA and data integrity](../../data-integrity-and-records/alcoa-and-data-integrity/index.qmd).

### 3. Retention of what was sent, and of the crosswalk

There are three different things to keep, and two different sources of rules:

- **The BECS records.** Regulated, retained under 21 CFR 606.160(d). See
  [retention across record types](../../data-integrity-and-records/retention-across-record-types/index.qmd).
  Nothing in this lesson changes that.
- **Copies of sent files, the ledger and the provenance record.** No regulation in our sources says
  how long an extract file must be kept, and module 2 left open whether it is a record under any
  regulation (Quality and regulatory affairs decide). The DUA is the practical source: it should
  state how long Lakeshore keeps each, and when it destroys them. The ledger and provenance record
  are small and cheap, and they are what let you answer a question years later. The files themselves
  are reproducible from BECS only if the mapping and source data are unchanged, which is exactly
  what provenance tells you.
- **The crosswalk.** It is the one item that can re-link a code to a donor. Keep it as long as the
  program might need Lakeshore to resolve a correction or a re-link, protect it as a CMDB item, and
  let the DUA say when it is destroyed. **Destroying the crosswalk is a privacy decision**: it makes
  the program's coded data unlinkable at Lakeshore. It is also irreversible. Make it explicitly, with
  the privacy officer.

Don't invent periods. The privacy officer, regulatory affairs and counsel set them with the program.
IT's job is to make whatever they pick enforceable: a retention rule on the file store, a destruction
step with a record of it, and an expiry review on the CMDB item.

A subtlety to flag: **destruction ends Lakeshore's copies, not the confidentiality obligation.** The
CoC decision treats protection as indefinite. A destroyed file with a ledger entry is still a file
that was sent.

### 4. Responding to data corrections

Module 2 said source errors are fixed in BECS under its controls, never in the extract. The DMS
angle: data that will be shared should be right, so corrections must be able to reach the program.
Whether it restates, flags or replaces is decided by the data specification (an open item from module
2). Whatever it picks, each correction should produce a **new run and a new ledger row that supersedes
the old one**, with the reason. And the correction reaches both the program's copy and any copy
already prepared for sharing. That second part is the program's job. Lakeshore's job is to say, in the
DUA, that it will notify and expects the program to propagate.

### 5. Answering "what did you send?"

Combine the above. When the hub, an IRB, a privacy complaint or an audit asks, you can produce: the
spec version, the mapping version, the run's signed QC, the ledger row with checksum, the DUA terms,
and the retention status. That is the evidence package.

## See it in one picture

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    L["Lakeshore<br/>EXT-21 limited data set<br/>under DUA"] -->|"transfer: ledger entry<br/>(file, spec version,<br/>mapping version, checksum)"| H["Hub / DCC<br/>(the NIH-funded performers)"]
    K[("Coded key crosswalk<br/>stays at Lakeshore")] -.-x|"never leaves"| H
    H --> V["Program's V2V database<br/>(source data retained)"]
    V --> Q{"Program decides what to share<br/>under its approved DMS Plan"}
    Q -->|"further de-identified<br/>under program's own process"| R["NIH-designated repository<br/>(e.g. BioLINCC for REDS-III)"]
    Q -->|"anything else"| X["Stays under DUA terms:<br/>no onward disclosure"]
    H -.->|"correction request<br/>or provenance question"| L
    L -.->|"fix in BECS, re-run,<br/>new ledger entry"| H
```

The BioLINCC node is the one documented example (the paper's REDS-III public-use data). Nothing in
our sources says the current round will use it.

## What an assessor or reviewer would look for

No FDA inspector asks about the DMS policy. A hub site visit, an IRB, the privacy officer or an
internal audit would. They look for:

- **The signed agreement and DUA**, with the repository clause either narrowed or struck. Bad answer:
  "It's NIH standard language."
- **The transfer ledger**, complete, with checksums and spec and mapping versions. Bad answer: "The
  logs are in the SFTP server," which doesn't tie to a spec version.
- **The provenance link** from a file to its mapping version and source fields.
- **The retention and destruction schedule** for files, ledger and crosswalk, and evidence it runs.
- **The record of corrections**, each linked to a BECS fix and a superseding run.
- **Evidence that no coded key or crosswalk ever left**, and the access list for the crosswalk.

## Common traps

1. **"The DMS policy binds us."** It binds NIH-funded researchers and institutions. Lakeshore is bound
   by what it signs. Read the agreement for passed-down terms.
2. **"Sharing means public."** The policy's own definition runs from "institutions" to "the broader
   public." A limited data set under a DUA is a restricted share. Public needs more de-identification.
3. **"The policy adds privacy protection."** It states that it doesn't introduce new human-participant
   protections. Privacy comes from the Common Rule, HIPAA and CoCs.
4. **"They keep it, so we don't have to."** The program retaining source data doesn't tell you
   what you sent, which mapping produced it, or whether a correction landed. Only your ledger does.
5. **"Retention means keep forever."** Retention is a decision with a date and a destruction step.
   Keeping a crosswalk indefinitely is a privacy risk too.

## What this means for your job

- **Read every agreement for passed-down terms.** Ask regulatory affairs to list each clause that
  obliges Lakeshore to follow "the program's plan" or "NIH policy." Each is a contract duty.
- **Ask the hub for the plan.** Which data does the program expect to share, where, in what form,
  and by when? If they can't say, that's your answer about how firm the clause is.
- **Build the ledger and provenance record into EXT-21 now.** Adding them after the first transfer
  means a gap you can't fill.
- **Put retention and destruction on the CMDB item,** with an owner and a review date for the file
  store and the crosswalk, set by the privacy officer, not by IT's disk budget.
- **Escalate** any proposal to share, publish or re-disclose beyond the named recipients, any request
  for the crosswalk, and any legal request about the data, to the privacy officer and counsel
  before IT acts.
- **Keep the tiers straight** in every email: NIH funding policy, HIPAA regulation, the agreement,
  Lakeshore's own policy.

## The Director's decision for RSH-0107

Recorded, with the privacy officer's concurrence:

> **Lakeshore accepts repository sharing only of data the program has further de-identified under
> the program's own process. It does not accept repository sharing of the limited data set, and
> never of Lakeshore's coded key or crosswalk.**
>
> 1. **DUA terms.** The data use agreement says, in terms: the recipient may not use or further
>    disclose the limited data set other than as the DUA permits; named recipients only; the same
>    restrictions bind any agents; no attempt to identify or contact individuals; and report any
>    unauthorized use or disclosure (45 CFR 164.514(e)(4)).
> 2. **Repository clause.** The page-six sentence is replaced with the narrowed version above. The
>    DUA asks the program to state its de-identification process and to pass Lakeshore's
>    limitations to any repository.
> 3. **Retention and destruction.** The DUA names how long each party keeps files, and requires
>    destruction terms for the limited data set. Periods are set by the privacy officer, regulatory
>    affairs and counsel. Destruction does not end the confidentiality commitments from module 3.
> 4. **IT build.** The transfer ledger and provenance record are built as part of EXT-21 (spec
>    version, mapping version, checksum, receipt, supersession), under change control, before the
>    first transfer.
> 5. **Corrections.** Source errors are fixed in BECS, produce a new run and a superseding ledger
>    row, and Lakeshore notifies the hub for propagation.
> 6. **Open questions to the hub, in writing:** is there an approved plan for this phase; what will
>    be shared, where and when; what de-identification process is used.

RSH-0107's condition 3 (written agreement and security terms) are now half-met: the data side is
decided here, and the security side is module 5.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: The medical director says Lakeshore must comply with the DMS policy because it joins an NIH-funded program. Is she right?

Not directly. The policy requires funded researchers and institutions to submit and follow a plan.
Our local copy's header says it isn't binding on a blood center that isn't an awardee or performing
under one. Lakeshore can still take on obligations by signing an agreement that passes plan terms
down, so you read the agreement. This is a **funding-policy, not a regulatory** answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does the DMS policy let the program put Lakeshore's limited data set in a public repository?

The policy doesn't decide that for Lakeshore. It expects researchers to account for legal, ethical
and technical limits, and says existing laws still apply. For a limited data set, 45 CFR 164.514(e)(4)
puts the permitted uses and recipients in the DUA, and the DUA may not authorize further disclosure
that would violate the Privacy Rule if done by the covered entity. Public sharing would require the
program to de-identify further. Lakeshore's DUA should say so.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Name three things a ledger row should let you prove two years from now.

Any three of: which spec version defined the file; which mapping version produced it; that the file
received is the file released (checksum); who received it and when; that a signed QC preceded
release; which later run, if any, superseded it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q4: Is there a regulation that says how long Lakeshore must keep an EXT-21 output file?

Not in any source we hold. 21 CFR 606.160(d) governs retention of the BECS product records, not the
extract. Whether the extract file is a record under any regulation was left to Quality and regulatory
affairs in module 2. The DUA and Lakeshore's own policy set the period. This is a "not a regulatory
requirement we can cite" answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q5: Explain to your CIO in two sentences what the NIH sharing policy means for us.

"NIH requires the funded research teams to plan and follow how they share data, and it doesn't make
Lakeshore a party unless our agreement says so. So we control what leaves through our data use
agreement, and IT's job is to keep a ledger and provenance record showing exactly what we sent and
how it was built."
:::

## Where this goes next

Module 5, security expectations for research data, turns the transfer, key and access decisions
made here and in module 3 into concrete controls, and applies NIH's controlled-access genomic-data
rules only where they genuinely apply. Genomic controlled-access data has its own rules (NIH's
NOT-OD-24-157), which don't automatically apply to EXT-21's donor, donation and component fields.
